```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("../setup.R")
docs_setup(legend = "bottom")
```

Intervals show supplied lower and upper bounds around a position. They can describe measurement uncertainty, variation among observations or uncertainty in a summary, depending on how the bounds were computed. This article draws intervals on three axes and summarises petal lengths by species. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html).

1. **Map** the centre and both bounds of each interval axis in `aes()`.

2. **Draw** capped bars, point ranges or boxes with `geom_errorbar_3d()`, `geom_pointrange_3d()` or `geom_crossbar_3d()`.

3. **Summarise** repeated observations with `stat_summary_3d()`.

## Example

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
```

### Drawing supplied bounds

Each row below describes a measured position and a stated half-width on every axis, in arbitrary units. [geom_errorbar_3d()](../reference/geom_errorbar_3d.html) draws a bar for each pair of bounds. The example widths are supplied values; the layer draws them without estimating their statistical meaning.

```{r supplied, fig.alt="Three measured points with capped intervals along x, y and z."}
measurements <- data.frame(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(2, 1, 3),
                           z = c(3, 4, 2))
ranges <- ggplot(measurements, aes(x, y, z = z,
  xmin = x - 0.2, xmax = x + 0.2,
  ymin = y - 0.3, ymax = y + 0.3,
  zmin = z - 0.5, zmax = z + 0.5))
ranges + geom_errorbar_3d(width = 0.12, cap_plane = "cross",
                           linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3, colour = "#2E6F9E") + coord_3d()
```

Cross-shaped caps extend in both directions perpendicular to each bar. The width is measured in transformed coordinate units along those directions. For a single z interval, `cap_plane = "xz"` puts the caps along x. A missing pair of bounds omits that axis; supply both endpoints for every interval that should appear.

| Geometry | Display |
|---|---|
| `geom_linerange_3d()` | Interval segments |
| `geom_errorbar_3d()` | Segments with endpoint caps |
| `geom_pointrange_3d()` | Segments and a centre point |
| `geom_crossbar_3d()` | Boxes with a line at the centre |

The same mappings can draw point ranges. Use them when the centre and extent are enough to read the interval. Joint uncertainty across axes needs a model of their dependence; three separate marginal intervals do not define a joint confidence region.

```{r point-ranges, fig.alt="The same three positions shown as points with uncapped intervals on all axes."}
ranges + geom_pointrange_3d(colour = "#2E6F9E", linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_3d()
```

### Summarising repeated observations

The iris table records petal lengths in centimetres for three species. [stat_summary_3d()](../reference/stat_summary_3d.html) summarises z within each group and each distinct x/y position. Its default summary is the mean plus or minus one standard error, calculated from the observations in that cell.

```{r means, fig.alt="Mean petal length with one-standard-error intervals for each iris species."}
flowers <- ggplot(iris, aes(Species, y = 0, z = Petal.Length)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = NULL) +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis_3d(n.dodge = 2))
flowers + stat_summary_3d(fun.data = mean_se, colour = "#2E6F9E",
                          linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(z = "Petal length (cm)", y = NULL) + coord_3d()
```

One standard error describes precision of the sample mean. To display the spread of observations, supply a summary such as the median with the first and third quartiles. The function returns columns named y, ymin and ymax, which the stat translates to the selected axis.

```{r quartiles, fig.alt="Median petal length with boxes spanning the first to third quartiles for each iris species."}
quartiles <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), names = FALSE)
  data.frame(y = q[2], ymin = q[1], ymax = q[3])
}
flowers + stat_summary_3d(fun.data = quartiles, geom = "crossbar",
                          width = 0.35, fill = "#2E6F9E") +
  labs(z = "Petal length (cm)", y = NULL) + coord_3d()
```

An explicit group mapping separates summaries that share a position. Discrete colour and fill mappings also define groups. Mapping a different group to every observation prevents pooling; a standard error then cannot be estimated from within-cell variation. Summaries use scale-transformed values, so applying a logarithmic scale changes the quantity being averaged. Compute summaries in original units before plotting when that is the intended quantity.

A cell with a single observation has no standard error. Its mean is drawn as
a point without bounds.

### Preparing a summary table

A precomputed table makes the bounds available for checking and reuse. The following table contains one row per species, with the mean and one-standard-error bounds in centimetres. Its named columns feed directly into the point-range layer.

```{r summary-table}
summary_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(iris, iris$Species), function(d) {
  mean_length <- mean(d$Petal.Length)
  se <- sd(d$Petal.Length) / sqrt(nrow(d))
  data.frame(species = d$Species[1], mean = mean_length,
             lower = mean_length - se, upper = mean_length + se)
}))
rownames(summary_table) <- NULL
summary_table
```

```{r precomputed, fig.alt="The precomputed species means and standard-error bounds drawn as point ranges."}
ggplot(summary_table, aes(species, y = 0, z = mean,
                          zmin = lower, zmax = upper)) +
  geom_pointrange_3d(colour = "#2E6F9E", linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = NULL) +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis_3d(n.dodge = 2)) +
  labs(z = "Petal length (cm)", y = NULL) + coord_3d()
```

[Positioning groups and observations](positions.html) shows how to separate groups within a cell. For fitted-mean uncertainty and observation-to-fit segments, use the model examples in [Surfaces, solids and fields](surfaces-solids.html#function-and-fitted-surfaces). Its ellipsoid examples describe three-dimensional spread and uncertainty in a mean.
